Issues.Title: Avoid StreamReader allocations in MultipartSection.ReadAsStringAsync
Issues.Body:

Makes `MultipartSection.ReadAsStringAsync` (used by `FormReader`/`FormFeature` for every multipart form field) skip the per-call `StreamReader` and its buffers for typical UTF-8 values.

## Description

Today each call allocates a `StreamReader` along with its 1 KB byte buffer, its char buffer and a `StringBuilder` for `ReadToEndAsync`. That's about 3.5 KB of garbage per form field, even for a 16-byte value.

With this change:
- **UTF-8 values (the default) in sections created by `MultipartReader`:** the body is read into an `ArrayPool` buffer. It starts at 4 KB and doubles up to a 64 KB cap. At EOF we decode it directly with `Encoding.GetString`, so only the result string is allocated (56 B for a small field, down from 3,512 B).
- **Other cases:** we fall back to the original `StreamReader` code, fed by the bytes already read and then the rest of the body. That covers:
  - non-UTF-8 charsets;
  - sections whose `Body` was set by the caller. Only the internal `MultipartReaderStream` ever sees the pooled buffer, and it only copies already-buffered data into it, so caller code can't observe the buffer or keep it after it's returned;
  - bodies over 64 KB;
  - any first read that could start with a byte order mark (lead byte `EF`/`FE`/`FF`/`00`);
  - a first read shorter than 3 bytes.

**Behavior is unchanged, including edge cases:**
- `StreamReader`'s BOM detection depends on read boundaries: it only detects on a read of ≥2 bytes, and it stays armed after shorter reads.
- The fast path only decodes directly when the first read already has ≥3 bytes and starts with a non-BOM byte. In that case `StreamReader` would have ruled out every BOM (and the UTF-8 preamble) on its first read, so it would have decoded the bytes as-is.
- In every other case, `StreamReader` sees the same read boundaries as before.
- Invalid UTF-8 produces the same replacement characters.

New tests compare the result against `StreamReader` reading the same stream with the same read pattern. They cover:
- BOMs and partial BOMs, including BOMs appearing after a 1- or 2-byte first read;
- invalid UTF-8;
- multi-byte characters that straddle buffer boundaries;
- 0 B to 200 KB bodies;
- short and trickling reads;
- charsets from Content-Type.

The tests pass both before and after the change. Removing the short-read guard makes 4 of them fail, so they do catch that case.

No public API changes.

### Benchmarks

New `MultipartSectionReadAsStringBenchmark` (WebUtilities microbenchmarks). It parses a multipart body with `MultipartReader` and calls `ReadAsStringAsync` for each section. The runs used local BenchmarkDotNet with MemoryDiagnoser, in 2 interleaved base/new rounds on a 2-vCPU VM; ranges are the two rounds.

| FieldCount | ValueLength | Mean (main) | Mean (PR) | Allocated (main) | Allocated (PR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 16 | 2.06–2.23 μs | 1.70–1.77 μs | 10 KB | 7 KB |
| 1 | 2000 | 3.27–3.50 μs | 2.22–2.43 μs | 18 KB | 11 KB |
| 1 | 10000 | 10.3–10.7 μs | 6.0–6.3 μs | 62 KB | 26 KB |
| 1 | 100000 | 201–209 μs | 206–235 μs (noise) | 410 KB | 410 KB |
| 5 | 16 | 7.6–8.2 μs | 5.4–5.6 μs | 31 KB | 14 KB |
| 5 | 2000 | 15.3–15.4 μs | 8.7–9.3 μs | 71 KB | 34 KB |
| 5 | 10000 | 50–53 μs | 26–27 μs | 270 KB | 112 KB |
| 5 | 100000 | 880–1029 μs | 975–981 μs (noise) | 2,039 KB | 2,032 KB |

Values over 64 KB take the `StreamReader` fallback, so they're neutral within noise; an earlier pair of rounds showed the same.

### Tests

- `dotnet test src/Http/WebUtilities/test`: 548 passed, including the 42 new `MultipartSectionStreamExtensionsTests`. Each parity case runs both a `MultipartReader` section (fast path) and a caller-provided body (`StreamReader` path), and checks both against `StreamReader` under identical read chunking. The new tests also pass on `main`.

Issues.Body:

Makes `HttpRequest.HasFormContentType` skip Content-Type parsing for non-form requests and stop allocating `HttpContext.Items`.

## Description

`HttpRequest.HasFormContentType` is called on many requests:
- MVC's form and form-file value provider factories, during model binding;
- Minimal API form binding;
- antiforgery.

It had two avoidable costs:

1. **Full Content-Type parse.** Every call ran `MediaTypeHeaderValue.TryParse`, which allocates the header value, the media type string and the parameter list. This happened even for requests that obviously aren't forms, such as `application/json; charset=utf-8`. Both form media types (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and `multipart/form-data`) contain `form`, so if the raw header doesn't contain `form` (OrdinalIgnoreCase, the same comparison used for the media type check), the parsed media type can't match. In that case we now return `false` without parsing. Any value that does contain `form` still goes through the existing parse, so results don't change.
2. **`HttpContext.Items` allocation.** `HasFormContentType` reads `Form`, which runs the antiforgery guard. The guard checked `Items.ContainsKey(...)` twice before it checked whether an invalid `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` was present, and that lazily allocated `ItemsFeature` + `ItemsDictionary` on every request. It now checks the feature first and only touches `Items` when the token is invalid. Both checks are side-effect-free reads, so swapping the order of the `&&` doesn't change behavior.

No public API changes.

### Benchmarks

Added `FormFeatureBenchmark` to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Microbenchmarks`. It creates a fresh `DefaultHttpContext` per op, so the lazy allocations show up. BenchmarkDotNet (InProcess, MemoryDiagnoser) on a 2-vCPU Linux VM, two interleaved A/B rounds. Both rounds reproduced. The `CreateContext` baseline, about 220–300 ns, is included in the times below.

| Content-Type | main | PR | Alloc delta main | Alloc delta PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | 407–418 ns | 327–335 ns | 112 B | 64 B |
| `application/json; charset=utf-8` | 749–764 ns | 403–432 ns | 336 B | 64 B |
| `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` | 610–622 ns | 539–547 ns | 160 B | 112 B |
| `multipart/form-data; boundary=…` | 745–778 ns | 653–675 ns | 336 B | 288 B |

"Alloc delta" is the number of bytes `HasFormContentType` allocates on top of creating the context, measured exactly with `GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread`. The remaining 64 B is the lazily created `FormFeature` itself.

### Tests

New `FormFeatureTests`:
- `HasFormContentType` results for null, empty, JSON, near-miss values (`text/plain; format=form`, `application/form`, `multipart/form-data-x`) and case/whitespace variants. All of them pass on `main` as well, which confirms the results are unchanged.
- The antiforgery guard still throws when the token is invalid and either middleware marker is set, and doesn't throw otherwise.
- `HasFormContentType` doesn't create an `IItemsFeature`. This fails on `main`.

Test runs:
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http.Tests`: 279 passed, 7 skipped.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Antiforgery.Test`: 185 passed.

Issues.Title: Kestrel: vectorize query string end search in HTTP/1.1 request line parsing

`HttpParser.TryParseRequestLine` finds the end of the query string with a scalar byte-by-byte loop that looks for the space before the HTTP version. This PR replaces that loop with `ReadOnlySpan<byte>.IndexOf(ByteSpace)`, which is vectorized. Stops hosting metrics from allocating `HttpContext.Items` on every request.

## Description

When the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting` metrics are enabled, `HostingApplicationDiagnostics.RequestEnd` calls `httpContext.Items.ContainsKey("__RequestUnhandled")`. When no endpoint is set, the shared `GetOriginalEndpoint` helper also reads `Items`. On `DefaultHttpContext`, `Items` is created lazily, so each request that never touched `Items` allocated an `ItemsFeature` and an `ItemsDictionary` (48 B) just to find out it was empty. Activity stop (`GetOriginalEndpoint`) had the same problem.

This PR adds a private `TryGetItem` helper. When the context's exact type is `DefaultHttpContext`, it reads `IItemsFeature` from the feature collection, and if no feature exists there are no items. For any other `HttpContext` type it falls back to `Items.TryGetValue`. Behavior stays the same:
- the same keys are checked;
- `ContainsKey` is replaced with `TryGetValue`, which has the same result;
- subclasses that override `Items` keep going through `Items`.

No public API changes.

Also added:
- `src/Hosting/Hosting/perf/Microbenchmarks` with `HostingApplicationBenchmark`, which runs a full `CreateContext` → `ProcessRequestAsync` → `DisposeContext` cycle through the real `HostingApplication`, with metrics on or off.
- Tests: a route tag from the `__OriginalEndpoint` fallback, and no `IItemsFeature` created for a request with metrics enabled. The second test fails on `main` and passes with this change.

### Benchmarks

BenchmarkDotNet (InProcess, MemoryDiagnoser) on a 2-vCPU Linux VM, two interleaved A/B rounds. Both rounds reproduced.

| MetricsEnabled | EndpointMatched | main | PR | Alloc main | Alloc PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| True | False | 320–353 ns | 272–286 ns | 48 B | 0 B |
| True | True | 415–424 ns | 348–369 ns | 72 B | 24 B |
| False | False/True | no change (noise) | no change (noise) | unchanged | unchanged |

The remaining 24 B in the endpoint case is the benchmark's own `EndpointFeature` from `SetEndpoint`.

Issues.Title: Vectorize FastPathTokenizer
Issues.Body:
# Vectorize FastPathTokenizer

Vectorize the slash search in `FastPathTokenizer.Tokenize`.

## Description

`FastPathTokenizer.Tokenize` is called by `DfaMatcher` on every request. It called `IndexOf('/')` once per segment, and since paths are usually several short segments, the per-call overhead of `IndexOf` dominated.

It now compares a `Vector128` of chars at a time and enumerates the slashes found in each vector (`ExtractMostSignificantBits` + `TrailingZeroCount`), with a scalar loop for the tail. It also returns early when the segment buffer fills up, and when `segments` is empty.

Output is identical to the old implementation. A new test exhaustively compares it against a reference implementation over all paths up to 17 chars made of `'a'` and `'/'` (so slashes land at every position, including vector boundaries) with segment buffers of 1, 2, 3 and 32. That covers `"/"`, trailing slashes, and buffers shorter than the number of segments. No public API changes.

### Benchmarks

Existing `FastPathTokenizer*Benchmark` microbenchmarks (`Implementation` method), BenchmarkDotNet in-process with MemoryDiagnoser, 3 interleaved A/B rounds. AMD EPYC 9V74, 2 vCPUs, .NET 12.0.0, x64.

| Small (`/hello/world/cool`) | 10.84 / 10.92 / 10.76 | 4.07 / 4.05 / 4.08 | **-63%** | 0 B → 0 B |
| Large (~190 chars, 32+ segments) | 275.7 / 275.9 / 275.7 | 41.10 / 40.71 / 40.64 | **-85%** | 0 B → 0 B |

| Empty (`/`) | 4.91 / 4.87 / 4.89 | 1.97 / 1.95 / 1.94 | -60% | 0 B → 0 B |

Issues.Title: Reuse work lists in DfaMatcherBuilder.ApplyPolicies
Issues.Body:
# Reuse work lists in DfaMatcherBuilder.ApplyPolicies

Avoid two `List<DfaNode>` allocations per DFA node when building the matcher.

## Description

`DfaMatcherBuilder.ApplyPolicies` runs for every node in the DFA (about 1.5M times for the Azure route set in the microbenchmarks) and allocated two `List<DfaNode>` per call, even when no node builder policy applies to the node. It now reuses two builder-owned lists, swapping them between policy passes, and clears both at the end of each call so no nodes are retained by the builder.

`ApplyPolicies` is only invoked from `root.Visit(ApplyPolicies)` (post-order traversal; the visitor runs after child traversal completes and does not recurse), and node builder policies only receive endpoint lists, so the shared lists are never re-entered. `DfaMatcherBuilder` is registered as transient and already holds other reused build-time state (`_assignments`, `_slots`).

No public API or behavior changes.

### Benchmarks

`src/Http/Routing/perf/Microbenchmarks`, `MatcherBuilderAzureBenchmark.Dfa` and `MatcherBuilderGithubBenchmark.Dfa`, `--config perflab` (in-process, MemoryDiagnoser), 15 iterations / 3 warmups, 3 interleaved before/after rounds on the same machine.

| Benchmark | | Round 1 | Round 2 | Round 3 | Allocated / op |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Azure | before | 3.658 s | 3.403 s | 3.457 s | 1,276,186,552 B |
| Azure | after | 3.381 s | 3.319 s | 3.177 s | 1,207,856,176 B (**-68.3 MB, -5.4%**) |
| GitHub | before | 828.4 us | 872.0 us | 836.3 us | 672,941 B |
| GitHub | after | 795.9 us | 890.0 us | 864.9 us | 638,289 B (**-5.1%**) |

Azure build time improves ~4% (median 3.457 s -> 3.319 s); GitHub time is within noise. The allocation reduction is deterministic.

Issues.Title: Kestrel: avoid name allocation and extra lookups when appending unknown request headers
Issues.Body:
Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 request header path for **unknown** headers (anything not in the generated known-header switch) did:

1. `name.GetHeaderName()` – allocates a string for the name every time
2. `GetInternedHeaderName(nameStr)` – hashes it again to swap in the interned name (`DNT`, `X-Requested-With`, `Sec-WebSocket-*`, `Proxy-Connection`, ...)
3. `Unknown.TryGetValue` + `Unknown[name] = ...` – two more hashes

This PR replaces that with `AppendUnknownHeader(ReadOnlySpan<byte> name, ReadOnlySpan<byte> value, bool)`:

- For names ≤ 64 chars, decode the ASCII name into a stack buffer and probe the interned-name set with a `HashSet<string>.AlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>` – no name allocation when the header is a well-known name.
- The interned string is passed to the encoding selector only when the selector is the default (which ignores the name) or the received casing matches exactly; otherwise a string with the received casing is still created, so custom `RequestHeaderEncodingSelector`s observe exactly what they did before.
- Append via `CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrAddDefault` – one dictionary lookup instead of two.
- Empty / too long / invalid names fall back to the existing `GetHeaderName()` path, so the same `BadHttpRequestException` (`InvalidCharactersInHeaderName`) is thrown.

The change is made in the code generator (`KnownHeaders.cs`), and `HttpHeaders.Generated.cs` is regenerated.

### Benchmarks
Local BenchmarkDotNet (InProcess, MemoryDiagnoser), 2 vCPU VM, interleaved base/PR rounds. Every PR round was faster than every base round.

| Benchmark | main | PR | Allocated main → PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| RequestParsingBenchmark.PipelinedLiveAspNet | 724 ns | 683 ns (**-5.6%**) | 58 B → 26 B |
| RequestParsingBenchmark.UnicodePipelined | ~900 ns | ~885 ns | 59 B → 27 B |
| RequestHeadersAppendBenchmark (InternedUnknown, 6 headers) | 653 / 602 / 599 ns | 472 / 504 / 461 ns (**-21%**) | 496 B → 144 B |
| RequestHeadersAppendBenchmark (InternedUnknownLowercase) | 730 / 618 / 617 ns | 498 / 469 / 470 ns (**-24%**) | 496 B → 144 B |
| RequestHeadersAppendBenchmark (CustomUnknown) | 580 / 556 / 560 ns | 530 / 473 / 476 ns (**-15%**) | 464 B → 464 B |

Each RequestHeadersAppendBenchmark cell lists the per-round results of 3 interleaved rounds. The remaining 144 B is the six value strings.
`RequestHeadersAppendBenchmark` is new in this PR; each case appends 6 unknown headers per request (Reset → Append ×6 → OnHeadersComplete). The LiveAspNet request includes `DNT`, which is an unknown-but-interned header.

### Tests
- New `HttpRequestHeadersTests` cover:
  - a null char in an unknown name still throws
  - interned names reuse the interned instance
  - the first received casing is preserved as the key
  - long names (63/64/65/1000 chars)
  - a custom encoding selector still receives the received name casing
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Tests`: 9921 passed. The 13 failures are IPv6/AddressBinder environment failures that also fail on main.
- `InMemory.FunctionalTests` (Http2Stream/Http3Stream/Http2Connection/Request/RequestHeader/BadHttpRequest/RequestHeaderLimits): 1038 passed, 0 failed.

### No API / behavior change
- Internal implementation only. No `PublicAPI.*.txt` changes and no new public APIs.
- Dictionary keys, value concatenation, exceptions and the name passed to custom encoding selectors are unchanged.

Issues.Body:
# Reduce HPACK dynamic table name hashing

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable. (Existing tests cover it; this is an internal refactor. Adds a benchmark.)
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Small perf change, no issue.)

Reduce header-name hashing (`string.GetHashCode()`, randomized Marvin) in `DynamicHPackEncoder`. Marvin was ~16% of self time in the KnownHeaders benchmark profile.

## Description

When the HTTP/2 response header encoder misses the dynamic table, `DynamicHPackEncoder.EncodeDynamicHeader` hashed the header name with `string.GetHashCode()` (randomized Marvin) up to three times:

1. `GetEntry`, the name+value lookup.
2. `ResolveDynamicTableIndex` → `CalculateDynamicTableIndex`, the name-only lookup when there's no static index.
3. `AddHeaderEntry`, the bucket for the new entry.

This change computes the hash once in `EncodeDynamicHeader` and passes it to all three methods. The lookup, indexing and eviction logic is unchanged, so the encoded bytes are identical. No public API changes.

Misses happen whenever response header values change between responses, for example `Date`, `ETag` or per-request custom headers. I added `HPackHeaderWriterBenchmark.BeginEncodeHeaders_ChangingValues` to cover that path: it uses 256 rotating header sets with unique values, so each header misses and is inserted, and the table evicts.

### Benchmarks

Local BenchmarkDotNet (`--config perflab`, in-process), 2 vCPU VM. Base and new were run interleaved. ChangingValues mean per round, 7 rounds each:

| Benchmark | main | PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| BeginEncodeHeaders_ChangingValues | 1122 / 1034 / 1125 / 1050 / 1008 / 1086 / 1055 ns (avg ~1069) | 1044 / 997 / 1037 / 1008 / 991 / 1014 / 1005 ns (avg ~1014) | **~-5%** (PR faster in 7/7 paired rounds) |
| BeginEncodeHeaders_KnownHeaders | 417 ns | 414 ns | noise |
| BeginEncodeHeaders_KnownHeaders_CustomEncoding | 495 ns | 498 ns | noise |
| BeginEncodeHeaders_UnknownHeaders | 413 ns* | 412 ns | noise |
| BeginEncodeHeaders_UnknownHeaders_CustomEncoding | 412 ns | 414 ns | noise |

\* one base outlier round (1225 ns) excluded. Allocations are zero in both.

The existing benchmarks reuse the same values, so they hit the table and show no change, as expected.

### Static-table name hash cache (second commit)

Profiling showed Marvin hashing of the header name as the largest single cost in the encode loop, even on dynamic-table hits. Response headers that have an HPACK static table index (`Content-Type`, `Server`, `Date`, ...) come from `HttpResponseHeaders`, whose enumerator always yields the same `HeaderNames` constant instance for a known header. Unknown headers always get static index -1. So `DynamicHPackEncoder` now keeps a small process-wide array, indexed by static table index, of immutable `(string name, int hash)` entries:

- A cached hash is used only when the name is `ReferenceEquals` to the cached string, so it always equals `name.GetHashCode()`. A different instance recomputes the hash and replaces the entry.
- Entries are immutable and written by a single reference store, so concurrent connections can race safely and harmlessly.
- Headers with no static index take a separate branch and call `GetHashCode()` directly; the cache lookup is `NoInlining` to keep that path unchanged.
- The array holds at most 61 framework string constants, so it can't hold user data across requests.

The empty-table fast path flagged in review is also restored: `ResolveDynamicTableIndex` returns -1 before hashing when the dynamic table is empty.

Paired interleaved rounds (base = first commit only, PR = all commits), 3 rounds:

| Benchmark | base | PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|

Read buffered lines directly in BufferedReadStream and trim multipart headers on spans

## Description

`BufferedReadStream.ReadLine`/`ReadLineAsync` allocated a `MemoryStream` (plus its 200-byte buffer) for every line and copied the line into it one byte at a time. `MultipartReader` calls it for every boundary remainder, every section header and the blank line that ends the headers, so that is roughly four `MemoryStream`s per section.

This PR adds a fast path. When the terminating CRLF is already in the internal buffer, it is found with a vectorized `IndexOf("\r\n"u8)` and the line is decoded directly from the buffer. If there is no CRLF in the buffer, or the line would exceed `lengthLimit`, the code falls back to the existing loop. That means lines spanning buffers, unterminated lines and the `Line length limit N exceeded.` exception behave exactly as before.

`MultipartReader.ReadHeadersAsync` also used `Substring(...).Trim()`, which allocates a second string when the value has a leading space (the common `Name: value` shape). It now uses `AsSpan(...).Trim().ToString()`.

# Skip processing lower-priority candidates once a match is found in DfaMatcher

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (No issue; this is a small internal perf change.)

Stop evaluating worse-scored candidates after a valid match in `DfaMatcher`.

## Description

Candidates in a DFA state are sorted by score, and lower is better. `DfaMatcher` now stops processing candidates under these conditions:

- the default endpoint selector fast path is in use (no `IEndpointSelectorPolicy`, default `EndpointSelector`)
- debug logging is off
- a valid candidate has already been found
- the next candidate has a worse (higher) score

`DefaultEndpointSelector` can never pick those candidates, so capturing their route values and running their complex segments and constraints is wasted work. The candidate-state span is truncated at that point before it is passed to the selector.

The following behavior is unchanged:

- **Equal-score ambiguity is still reported.** Candidates with the same score as the first match are still processed, so `AmbiguousMatchException` still fires. Once a second valid candidate with the same score is found, skipping is turned off and every remaining candidate is processed, so the exception message (which lists all valid candidates, including lower-priority ones) is identical to before.
- **Higher-priority invalid candidates don't stop the scan.** If the best-scored candidate fails its constraints, processing continues until a valid one is found.
- **Debug logging** still processes and logs every candidate.
- **Custom selectors and endpoint selector policies** still see the full candidate set.

### Results

Local BenchmarkDotNet, in-process, Release, Server GC, on a noisy 2-vCPU AMD EPYC VM. I ran interleaved A/B rounds (main, then branch, repeated) and report the median of per-round means.

| Benchmark | main | PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 ordered candidates `/products/{id:int\|guid\|alpha\|minlength(1)\|}` in one state, first matches (`/products/17`) | 327 ns / 704 B | 137 ns / 256 B | **−58% time, −64% alloc** |
| Same state, third candidate matches (`/products/abc`) | 333 ns / 704 B | 274 ns / 480 B | **−18% time, −32% alloc** |
| `MatcherAzureBenchmark.Dfa`, per request | 330 ns / 327 B | 327 ns / 265 B | neutral time, −19% alloc |
| `MatcherGithubBenchmark.Dfa`, per request | 168 ns / 176 B | 162 ns / 145 B | neutral time, −18% alloc |

The first two rows come from a temporary benchmark that isn't part of this PR, because the existing route-set benchmarks rarely put multiple differently scored candidates in one state. Each endpoint has `order` 0–4, and every request runs the same state's five candidates. I ran 5 rounds × 15 iterations for those rows and 3 rounds × 15 iterations for Azure and GitHub. Per-round ranges didn't overlap for the first two rows: main 317–333 ns vs PR 133–142 ns, and main 327–335 ns vs PR 268–291 ns.

Issues.Title: Coalesce small writes in BufferedTextWriter (static SSR)
Issues.Body:
## Description

> **Stacked on #70139.** This branch contains #70139's two commits. Please review only the last commit, f542f082 ("Coalesce small writes in BufferedTextWriter"). I'll rebase once #70139 merges.

Static SSR (`EndpointHtmlRenderer`) writes HTML through `BufferedTextWriter`, and `StaticHtmlRenderer` emits it as many tiny writes: `<`, element names, attribute names, `="`, quotes, and the fragments from `HtmlEncoder.Encode`. Today each of those writes:
- allocates its own 32-byte `TextChunk` slot, with new `TextChunkPage`s every 256 writes and every flush;
- becomes a separate `WriteAsync` call on the underlying writer at flush time.

With a 100-row table, writing to a `BufferedTextWriter` cost about 4.5x as much as writing the same HTML to a `StringWriter` (~135 µs vs ~30 µs).

This change:
- Copies chars, spans, strings of up to 128 chars, and formatted ints into per-list, reusable 1024-char pages.
- Merges adjacent copied writes into a single `CharArraySegment` chunk, so a page of text becomes one `WriteAsync`.
- Keeps holding longer strings (for example, large markup blocks) by reference, as before.
- Keeps the char pages per `TextChunkListBuilder`, so the list being flushed is never touched by writes to the other list. Pages are reused after `Clear()`.
- Formats `Write(int)` at write time with `TryFormat` and the writer's `FormatProvider`, falling back to the existing int chunk.

### Benchmarks

Local BenchmarkDotNet, InProcess, 3 interleaved rounds against #70139's head. Ranges show min–max over the rounds.

| Benchmark | Before | After | Δ time | Δ alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `HtmlRendererBenchmark.WriteHtmlToBufferedWriter` (100-row table, new) | 134.6–139.3 µs / 216 KB | 51.7–56.5 µs / 39 KB | **−62%** | **−82%** |
| `BufferedTextWriterBenchmark` Flushes=1 | 8.39–8.71 µs / 30 KB | 6.88–7.03 µs / 19 KB | −19% | −37% |
| `BufferedTextWriterBenchmark` Flushes=50 (streaming) | 401–426 µs / 1113 KB | 316–323 µs / 423 KB | −23% | −62% |

I also tried a single doubling `char[]` instead of fixed pages. It was faster with 50 flushes, but it allocated more with a single flush (30 → 38 KB), so I went with pages.

- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints.Tests`: 889 passed, 0 failed.
- New tests:
  - adjacent copied writes are coalesced, with an exact underlying write count;
  - copied data is isolated from later mutation of the source array;
  - text larger than one page, and content split across many pages;
  - reuse after `Clear()`;
  - long and short strings, ints (including `int.MinValue`), null and empty strings.
- Updated `TextChunk` and `TextChunkPage` tests for the new segment representation.

# Avoid resolving the default hub activator from DI for every hub invocation

- [x] Read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).

- [x] Include inline documentation where applicable.

Cut the per-invocation DI cost of creating hubs with the default activator.

## Description

`IHubActivator<>` is registered as scoped (`TryAddScoped(typeof(IHubActivator<>), typeof(DefaultHubActivator<>))`). `DefaultHubDispatcher` creates a new scope for every hub invocation (and for `OnConnectedAsync`, `OnDisconnectedAsync` and `OnAuthenticationRefreshedAsync`) and resolves the activator from it. That scoped resolution is often the only thing that populates the scope's resolved-services dictionary, so each invocation also paid for the dictionary's buckets and entries, plus the DI lookup.

The dispatcher now resolves the activator through DI the first time, as before. It switches to constructing `new DefaultHubActivator<THub>(scope.ServiceProvider)` directly, which is the same object DI would create, only when two things hold:
- the resolved instance is the internal `DefaultHubActivator<THub>`, and
- the registration snapshot shows it's the unchanged default. `AddSignalRCore` registers an internal `HubActivatorRegistrations` singleton that's built after the container and reads the non-keyed `IHubActivator<>` descriptors: the last open-generic one must be `DefaultHubActivator<>`, and there must be no closed `IHubActivator<THub>` registration.

Custom activators, factories (including ones that sometimes return the default), decorators and per-hub overrides keep being resolved from DI on every call.

Hub creation and release are unchanged. `DefaultHubActivator` still resolves `THub` from the scoped provider when it's registered, or creates it with `ActivatorUtilities` and disposes it on release. No public API changes.

When hub constructors resolve other scoped services, the scope's dictionary is allocated anyway. The saving in that case is just the DI lookup for the activator.

Stop allocating a new target string for every invocation the .NET client receives.

## Description

The server binder already implements `IInvocationBinder.GetTarget` to return a cached method name, but the client's binder (`HubConnection.ConnectionState`) used the default implementation, which returns `null`. As a result, the JSON and MessagePack protocols allocated a new `string` for the target of every invocation the client received.

- `HubConnection.ConnectionState` (`#if NET` only) now implements `GetTarget`. It decodes the UTF-8 target into a stack buffer, capped at 256 bytes, and looks up the registered handler name with `ConcurrentDictionary.GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>()`. On a match it returns the existing key. Unknown or oversized targets return `null`, and the protocol falls back to allocating, as before.
- `JsonHubProtocol` now passes the raw target bytes to `GetTarget` only when `!reader.ValueIsEscaped`. `ValueSpan` holds the still-escaped bytes, so an escaped target such as `"\u004Dethod"` could otherwise be matched against a literally named handler. Client handler names are arbitrary strings, so this matters once the client implements `GetTarget`. Escaped targets fall back to `reader.GetString()`.

No public API changes.

## Benchmark

Rounds were interleaved: base, tgt, base, tgt. The benchmark's `json` parameter uses `NewtonsoftJsonHubProtocol`, which doesn't call `GetTarget`, so it's unaffected (allocations unchanged).

## Description

`DefaultHubDispatcher` resolves the **scoped** `IHubActivator<THub>` from a new service scope for every invocation, plus `OnConnectedAsync`, `OnDisconnectedAsync` and `OnAuthenticationRefreshedAsync`. With this change, the dispatcher resolves the activator from DI the first time, as before, and records whether the container produced `DefaultHubActivator<THub>`. If it did, later calls construct `new DefaultHubActivator<THub>(scope.ServiceProvider)` directly. The scoped provider is the same one, so hub construction, scoped dependencies, `Release` and disposal semantics don't change. Custom activators are still resolved from DI on every call. Because the default type is internal, user registrations can't produce it.

Issues.Title: Reset BufferedTextWriter char segment buffer between flushes
Issues.Body:
## Description

`BufferedTextWriter` (used for static SSR and streaming rendering output) stores every `char[]`/span write in a single `StringBuilder`. `HtmlEncoder` uses these writes for any text that needs encoding, such as `&`, quotes, `<`, or non-ASCII characters. The builder was never cleared, and `FlushAsync` called `ToString()` on it every time. With streaming rendering, which flushes once per render batch, each flush therefore copied all encoded text written so far in the response. The cost is quadratic in the number of flushes, and the memory is held for the lifetime of the response.

Changes:
- Each `TextChunkListBuilder` owns its own segment `StringBuilder`. The two lists alternate while a flush is in progress, so writes during an in-flight flush don't affect the list being flushed. Each list's buffer is reset after its content has been flushed.
- The reset is deferred until the next segment write. `StringBuilder.Clear()` on a multi-chunk builder allocates a consolidated buffer, which would be wasted after the final flush.
- Added a `Write(ReadOnlySpan<char>)` override, which avoids `TextWriter`'s rent-copy-`Write(char[])` fallback. `HtmlEncoder` calls this overload.

### Benchmark

New `BufferedTextWriterBenchmark` in `src/Components/Components/perf`. Each flush writes 100 `<td>` cells, half of which need HTML encoding. Results are from BenchmarkDotNet InProcess on a 2 vCPU Linux VM, 3 interleaved rounds.

Reuse per-endpoint candidate arrays across DFA states in `DfaMatcherBuilder`.

## Description

The same endpoint usually appears in many DFA states. For example, a parameter segment is reachable through every literal sibling. Each time, `DfaMatcherBuilder.CreateCandidate` recomputed and reallocated the slots, captures, complex segments and constraints arrays, even though they depend only on the endpoint. This change caches them per endpoint while `Build()` runs and shares the arrays between states. Only the score is per state, so cached entries are copied with a new score through a new `Candidate(in Candidate, int score)` constructor.

Sharing is safe because `DfaMatcher` never mutates these arrays. It copies `Slots` into a new per-request array before writing captures, and it only reads `Captures`, `ComplexSegments` and `Constraints`. The cache is scoped to a single `Build()` call and is cleared in a `finally` block.

**Why some inline constraints are excluded:** If a constraint is created from inline text (for example `{p:custom}`) and isn't on the known-cacheable allow list (`ICachableParameterPolicy`, with `OptionalRouteConstraint` unwrapped), it may be stateful, such as a user constraint that counts evaluations. `DfaMatcherBuilder`'s parameter-policy factory already declines to share those instances between routes for this reason. Today each DFA state gets its own instance, so endpoints that use such constraints aren't cached and still get fresh instances per state, as before. Policy instances supplied on the route pattern are still shared, because they're already the same object in every state. This applies only when the factory returns that exact instance, optionally wrapped in `OptionalRouteConstraint`. If a custom `ParameterPolicyFactory` returns a different object, it's treated as non-cacheable.

On the Azure set, `CreateCandidate` is called about 995K times per build and about 647K of those calls are now cache hits. The GitHub set has only 128 hits out of 564 calls, so the gain there is negligible. A control build with the cache disabled measured in the same range (median 572 µs).

# Avoid per-header allocations in SignalR hub protocols

Removes allocations on every header read and write in the MessagePack and JSON hub protocols.

## Description

Invocation headers are on the hot path whenever the .NET client has distributed tracing enabled, because it injects `traceparent`/`tracestate` into every invocation.

- **MessagePack read:** `ReadHeaders` built two interpolated strings per header (`$"headers[{i}].Key"` / `.Value`) only to use them in an exception message. The field name is now formatted only when reading fails, and the error messages stay the same.
- **MessagePack and JSON write:** `Headers` is typed as `IDictionary<string, string>`, so `foreach` boxed the enumerator. When the instance is a `Dictionary<string, string>` (what both protocols and the client create), it's now enumerated directly. Other implementations still use the interface path.

Issues.Title: Use ulong.TryFormat for Content-Length values >= 1000 in Kestrel
Issues.Body:
# Use ulong.TryFormat for Content-Length values >= 1000 in Kestrel

Faster HTTP/1.1 Content-Length header writing for values >= 1000

## Description

`BufferExtensions.WriteNumeric` (used by `HttpResponseHeaders.CopyToFast` to write `Content-Length`) handles values < 1000 inline, but anything larger, which covers most real response bodies, went through `WriteNumericMultiWrite`. That path reads a `[ThreadStatic]` scratch array, runs a div/mod-by-10 loop, and then copies the digits into the output.

This change formats directly into the output span with `ulong.TryFormat` (UTF-8, invariant). Only when the remaining span is too small does it fall back to a `stackalloc` buffer plus `BufferWriter.Write`. That fallback lives in its own non-inlined method so the common path skips the stackalloc prologue, and it keeps the existing behavior of filling the tail of the current span. The `[ThreadStatic]` scratch array is removed. `BufferWriter.Write`/`WriteMultiBuffer` now take `scoped ReadOnlySpan<byte>`; they never store the span, and this is what allows passing a stackalloc'd span.

I also added `BufferWriterWriteNumericBenchmark` (and a `BufferWriterWriteAsciiBenchmark` companion) to Kestrel's Microbenchmarks.

### Benchmark

`BufferWriterWriteNumericBenchmark.WriteNumeric` (BDN InProcess/perflab config, 2 vCPU Linux VM, 2 interleaved base/PR rounds, 1000 ops per invoke):

| 421 | 2.23–2.27 ns | 2.22–2.25 ns | = |
| 4,096 | 9.66–9.76 ns | 5.03–5.05 ns | **-48%** |
| 1,048,576 | 12.30–12.37 ns | 6.97–7.07 ns | **-43%** |
| 123,456,789,012 | 17.06–17.13 ns | 9.80–9.90 ns | **-43%** |

No allocations before or after.

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)

Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "[Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time" (#537)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and MVC API analyzers are deprecated
Issues.Body:
## Description

The `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` MSBuild property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. When `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will now emit warning `ASPDEPR007`.

## Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

## Previous behavior

Previously, developers could set `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` in their Web SDK projects to enable MVC API analyzers without any warnings or deprecation notices.

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

The project would build successfully without any deprecation warnings.

## New behavior

Starting in .NET 10 Preview 7, when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will emit warning `ASPDEPR007`:

```
warning ASPDEPR007: The IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
```

The analyzers will continue to function, but developers will receive this deprecation warning during compilation.

## Type of breaking change

- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

## Reason for change

## Reason for change

The MVC API analyzers were originally introduced to help keep return types and attributes in sync for API controllers, ensuring consistency between method signatures and their corresponding OpenAPI documentation. These analyzers provided compile-time validation to catch mismatches between declared return types and the actual types returned by controller actions.

However, with the introduction of Minimal APIs and the `TypedResults` pattern, the .NET ecosystem has evolved toward a more type-safe approach for API development. `TypedResults` provides compile-time guarantees about response types without requiring additional analyzers, making the MVC API analyzers redundant for modern .NET applications. In .NET 10, `TypedResults` are supported in controller-based APIs.

**Previous approach with MVC API analyzers:**
```csharp
[HttpGet]
[ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)]
[ProducesResponseType(404)]
public async Task<ActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    if (product == null)
        return NotFound(); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType(404)
    
    return Ok(product); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)
}
```

**Or with controller actions using TypedResults:**
```csharp
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    return product == null 
        ? TypedResults.NotFound() 
        : TypedResults.Ok(product);
}
```

The `TypedResults` pattern eliminates the need for separate analyzers because the return type itself (`Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>`) explicitly declares all possible response types at compile time. This approach is more maintainable, provides better IntelliSense support, and automatically generates accurate OpenAPI documentation without additional tooling.

As the .NET ecosystem continues to embrace `TypedResults` as the recommended pattern for API development, the MVC API analyzers have become obsolete and are being deprecated to streamline the development experience.

## Recommended action

Developers should:

1. **Remove the deprecated property**: Remove `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` from your project files to eliminate the warning.

2. **Suppress the warning temporarily**: If you need to continue using the deprecated analyzers temporarily, you can suppress the warning:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ASPDEPR007</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

3. **Migrate to TypedResults**: Migrate to the `TypedResults` pattern documented above to ensure better consistency between application behavior and OpenAPI documentation.

## Affected APIs

- MSBuild property: `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers`
- Associated MVC API analyzers included when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is `true`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Forwarded Headers Middleware Now Ignores X-Forwarded-* Headers from Unknown Proxies
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, the Forwarded Headers Middleware will ignore all `X-Forwarded-*` headers from proxies that are not explicitly configured as trusted.

### Version

.NET 8

### Previous behavior

Previously, the middleware, when not configured to use `X-Forwarded-For`, would process `X-Forwarded-Prefix`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers from any source, potentially allowing malicious or misconfigured proxies/clients to spoof these headers and affect your application's understanding of client information.

### New behavior

With this change, only headers sent by known, trusted proxies (as configured via `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies` and `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownNetworks`) will be processed. Headers from unknown sources will be ignored.

**This is a breaking change**: If your deployment relied on forwarded headers from proxies not configured in your application's trusted proxy list, those headers will no longer be honored.

This can cause behavior like infinite redirects if you're using the Https redirection middleware and using TLS termination in your proxy. Or authentication to fail if using TLS termination and expecting an https request.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The change was made for security hardening, as the proxy and IP lists weren't being applied in all cases.

### Recommended action

- **Review your deployment topology:**  
  Ensure that all legitimate proxy servers in front of your app are properly added to `KnownProxies` or `KnownNetworks` in your `ForwardedHeadersOptions` configuration.
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownProxies = { IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_PROXY_IP") }
  });
  ```
  Or, for a network:
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownNetworks = { new IPNetwork(IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_NETWORK_IP"), PREFIX_LENGTH) }
  });
  ```

- **If you wish to enable previous behavior:**  
  You may need to relax your configuration, but this is **not recommended** due to security risks. You can do this by clearing the `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` lists in `ForwardedHeadersOptions` to allow any proxy or network to forward these headers.

You can also set the `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` environment variable to true, which clears the lists and enables `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto`.

For applications targeting .NET 9.0 or less, you can set the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides.IgnoreUnknownProxiesWithoutFor` [AppContext](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/runtime-libraries/system-appcontext) switch to `"true"` or `1` to get back to the previous behavior. Alternatively, set the `MICROSOFT_ASPNETCORE_HTTPOVERRIDES_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_PROXIES_WITHOUT_FOR` environment variable.

> [!Note]
> In cloud environments, the proxy IP(s) can change over the lifetime of the app and `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` is sometimes used to make forwarded headers work.

### References

- [Forwarded Headers Middleware documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/proxy-load-balancer)

### Affected APIs

`UseForwardedHeaders();`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: dev cert export no longer creates folder
Issues.Body:
### Description

When you export the ASP.NET Core development certificate (used to enable https in local development), it will no longer create the directory into which the certificate is being exported, if that directory doesn’t already exist.

This change first appears in 8.0.10 and 9.0 RC1.

### Version

.NET 8 GA

### Previous behavior

```
dotnet dev-certs https -ep C:\NonExistent\cert.pfx
```

If `C:\NonExistent\` did not exist when the command was run, it would be created (with permissions inherited from the containing directory).

### New behavior

The target directory must exist or the export will fail with a message like `There was an error exporting the HTTPS developer certificate to a file.`

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The development certificate is exported with its private key, so unauthorized access can be very problematic.  It may, nevertheless, be necessary to make it readable to multiple accounts - e.g. if the consuming process will not be run as the current user.  Rather than attempting to determine (and securely establish) permissions for the target directory, `dotnet dev-certs` require that it already exist.

### Recommended action

Create the target directory (with appropriate permissions) before invoking `dotnet dev-certs`.

### Affected APIs

This functionality is not presently exposed via an API - it is invoked from the command line.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Handling of middleware types with multiple constructors
Issues.Body:
### Description

Formerly, when a middleware type with multiple satisfiable constructors was instantiated from the dependency injection container, the one with the most parameters would be used.  Now that only happens if the dependency injection container implements [`IServiceProviderIsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.iserviceproviderisservice).

### Version

.NET 9 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Formerly, the first constructor was preferred (when both were satisfied) because it has more parameters.


Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey has a slightly altered meaning
Issues.Body:
### Description

`DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey` no longer reflects whether the default key is close to its expiration time.

### Version

.NET 9 Preview 3

### Previous behavior

It was an undocumented, but consistent, feature of the API that `ShouldGenerateNewKey` would be true if the default key was within two days (an over-simplification) of its expiration time.  The amount of lead time was based on the polling interval of `ICacheableKeyRingProvider`, which was not something `IDefaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy` should have depended upon (since, for example, alternative implementations would probably not be aware of these details).

### New behavior

If `ShouldGenerateNewKey` is true, it now indicates that either there is no default key or that for some other policy reason (i.e. in a specialized implementation of `IDefaultKeyResolver`, a new key should be generated.  The `ICacheableKeyRingProvider` will make its own decision about whether the expiration time is close enough to warrant generating a new key.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

First, we wanted to change the logic around key generation near expiration time and, second, this makes it more straightforward to implement a custom `IDefaultKeyResolver`.

Note that the documentation for this type already states that "This API supports infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases."

### Recommended action

If you have an `IDefaultKeyResolver` implementation that tries to replicate the expiry logic, that logic can be removed (however, leaving it is fine as well).

If you were consuming `IDefaultKeyResolver` directly, for the express purpose of determining whether expiration was pending and that continues to be important, you can the default key's `ExpirationDate` property directly.

### Affected APIs

Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal.DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Minimal APIs consuming IFormFile or IFormFileCollection parameters require anti-forgery checks
Issues.Body:
### Description

Minimal API endpoints that consume an `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` will now be opted-in to requiring anti-forgery token validation using the new anti-forgery middleware.

### Version

.NET 8 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did not require anti-forgery validation.

### New behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did require anti-forgery validation. An exception will be thrown if the anti-forgery middleware is not registered for an API that defines these input types.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Anti-forgery token validation is a recommended security precaution for APIs that consume data from a form.

### Recommended action

Users can opt out of anti-forgery validation for specific endpoints by using the `DisableAntiforgery` method like so:

```csharp
var app = WebApplication.Create();

app.MapPost("/", (IFormFile formFile) => ...)
  .DisableAntiforgery();

app.Run();
```

### Affected APIs

None.
